content: 1. The hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 is involved in the metabolism of certain drugs. Exercise caution and monitor patients when co-administering drugs that interact with this enzyme. No dosage adjustment is typically required, but regular monitoring of blood pressure, serum potassium, edema, and kidney function is recommended when sparsentan is used with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors. 2. Quinupristin/dalfopristin can increase the levels or effects of sufentanil by altering CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is minor or unknown, but close monitoring is advised. Co-administration of sufentanil SL with any CYP3A4 inhibitor may elevate sufentanil plasma concentrations, potentially leading to prolonged or severe adverse effects, including life-threatening respiratory depression. Monitor closely. 3. Quinupristin/dalfopristin increases the levels or effects of sunitinib, tacrolimus, tadalafil, temsirolimus, tezacaftor, theophylline, tinidazole, tipranavir, tolterodine, trazodone, triamcinolone acetonide injectable suspension, triazolam, vardenafil, verapamil, vinblastine, vincristine, vincristine liposomal, vinorelbine, voclosporin, zaleplon, zanubrutinib, ziprasidone, zolpidem, and zonisamide by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. Adjust dosages as necessary for specific drugs, especially when co-administered with moderate or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. 4. Co-administration of tazemetostat with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. If unavoidable, reduce the tazemetostat dose as per dosage modification guidelines and monitor closely. 5. Quinupristin/dalfopristin decreases the efficacy of the live typhoid vaccine due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Administration of live bacterial vaccines should be delayed until antibiotic therapy is completed. 6. Prolonged use of quinupristin/dalfopristin may result in fungal or bacterial superinfections. It inhibits the metabolism of drugs processed by CYP3A4 and may prolong the QTc interval when used with cisapride. Prescribing this drug without a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of drug-resistant bacteria development. 7. Common adverse effects include local pain (40-44%), inflammation at the infusion site (38-42%), hyperbilirubinemia (3-35%), local edema (17-18%), infusion site reactions (12-13%), arthralgia (<1-8%), nausea (3-5%), myalgia (<1-5%), vomiting (3-4%), anemia (3%), diarrhea (3%), increased LDH (3%), rash (3%), pain (2-3%), headache (2%), increased CPK (2%), increased GGT (2%), pruritus (2%), thrombophlebitis (2%), hyperglycemia (1%), and hypersensitivity to the drug or other streptogramins (e.g., pristinamycin, virginiamycin). 8. Quinupristin/dalfopristin is not active against Enterococcus faecalis. Caution is advised in patients with hepatic impairment, as the drug may cause arthralgias, myalgias, hyperbilirubinemia, and phlebitis. 9. The drug is excreted primarily in feces (75-77% as unchanged drug and metabolites) and urine (15-19%). It has a clearance rate of 72 L/hr/kg. 10. Reconstitution of the drug involves adding 5 mL of D5W or SWI to a 500 mg vial to achieve a 100 mg/mL solution. Do not shake; swirl gently to dissolve while minimizing foam formation. Dilute the reconstituted solution within 30 minutes and administer in at least 250 mL of D5W for peripheral administration. Increase the volume to 500 mL or 750 mL if necessary to reduce venous irritation. For central line infusions, a volume of 100 mL may be used. Do not freeze the solution. Flush with D5W before and after administration, as the drug is incompatible with saline. Complete the infusion over one hour to minimize toxicity. 11. If severe venous irritation occurs during peripheral administration, consider increasing the infusion volume, changing the infusion site, or using a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) or central venous catheter. 12. Unopened vials should be refrigerated.
